list.listitem: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a heterogeneous group of genetic connective-tissue disorders resulting in bone fragility for which there is no curative treatment. B
Diagnosis is typically based on a family history of bone fragility, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hyperlaxity of ligaments, and skin or hearing impairment presenting in the first two decades of life. C

Management should be provided within a multidisciplinary team including orthopedics to manage fractures and bone deformities; physical therapy to assist with mobility, independence and pain control; dental expertise to manage dentinogenesis imperfecta, and other specialists as needed. C
Patients with thoracic scoliosis exceeding 60° have severe reductions in pulmonary function and quality of life. B
IV pamidronate increases bone mineral density (BMD) but has not been clearly shown to reduce fracture incidence. B

background.definition: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), often referred to as "brittle bone disease", is a group of genetic bone disorders characterized by connective tissue defects or modifications, leading to decreased development of bone mass and increased bone fragility. Bones in affected patients are often collagen deficient, or contain "poor quality" collagen, and are very weak, fracturing with minimal trauma. The spectrum of OI is divided into 9 different subtypes (Types I-IX) according to clinical features and genetics, which range from mild forms that present in middle age as premature osteoporosis, to perinatal lethality. The most prevalent types are autosomal dominant and caused by primary defects in type I collagen; the less prevalent, autosomal recessive forms are caused by a deficiency in proteins necessary for post-translational modification of type I procollagen. OI demonstrates no preferential gender, race or ethnic distribution, and may exhibit an array of associated features including short stature, characteristic "blue sclera", macrocephaly, dentinogenesis imperfecta (defective formation and calcification of dentin), hearing loss and cardiovascular, pulmonary or neurologic complications.

list.listitem: OI is the most common inheritable connective tissue disorder.

Incidence of recognizable forms of autosomal dominant OI at birth is approximately 1/20,000-30,000 births. In a recent population-based dataset for births from all resident women in Utah, the incidence of OI was 0.79 per 10,000.
The carrier frequency of autosomal recessive Type VIII OI is 1/200-300 in African Americans.
A primary care physician in full-time practice will rarely see a patient with severe OI.

Many children with OI are investigated as victims of abuse, as frequent fractures are characteristic of OI, and bone disease is a diagnosis of exclusion in child abuse. In one convenience sample of 33 children with fractures diagnosed with OI at a mean age of 7.1 months (range: 1-23 months), 70% of children had been removed from the family and older siblings were removed in 62% of cases; this was despite a family history supportive of OI in about half.
Craniofacial and craniocervical deformities are known findings of OI and can lead to life threatening complications.

Dentinogenesis imperfecta, translucent, discolored, fragile teeth, is a common feature of many types of OI. In an adult population of 94 patients with OI in Norway, 17% had clinical signs of dentinogenesis imperfecta.

Approximately half of patients with OI develop progressive hearing loss, typically presenting in adulthood. The hearing impairment is related to abnormal bone quality, and usually begins as a conductive loss which ultimately progresses to a mixed hearing loss.
Cardiovascular and respiratory manifestations, due to the skeletal deformities, are responsible for the majority of morbidity and mortality of OI.

In one case series, the incidence of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis was found to be about twice that of the general population (8.2% (9 of 110) vs. 2.6% to 4.0% for spondylolysis and 10.9% (12 of 110) vs. 4.2% for spondylolisthesis).
Maintenance of body mass composition and nutritional support related to bone health are important in modifying OI risk factors.
Patients with OI have normal intellect.

Most cases of OI (85%-90%) are caused by an autosomal dominant defect in the genes coding for the two chains that comprise type I collagen (COL1A1 and COL1A2), the major protein of the extracellular matrix of bone, skin and tendon (Types I-VI). However, Types II and III can have autosomal recessive inheritance.
More than 800 independent dominant negative mutations have been identified, complicated by multiple examples of variable expression, causing a weakened higher-order collagen structure.

The remaining 10%-15% of cases (Types VII-XIX) are primarily autosomal recessive forms leading to a deficiency of one of the components of the endoplasmic-reticulum resident collagen prolyl 3-hydroxylation complex, important in bone formation (e.g. genes LEPRE1, CRTAP and PPIB). Next-generation sequencing technology has provided greater understanding of OI-causing genes and novel pathogenic variants including non-collagenous genes, those encoding proteins involved in collagen biosynthesis, or transcription factors and signaling molecules related to bone cell differentiation and mineralization.
Recently, an X-linked gene for OI has been identified (OI type XIX).

The spectrum of OI syndromes are characterized by clinical findings and genetic mutations (see Differential Diagnosis table). Most forms of OI fit into the original Sillence subtypes (I-IV) based on the clinical features and disease severity ().

The primary genetic defect in OI is one of qualitative (mutated proteins combine and result in defective protein ultrastructures) or quantitative (decreased amounts produced) reduction in type I collagen, leading to bone fragility. Type I collagen is an important structural protein in both endochondral and intramembranous ossification. The degree of histologic change in the collagen structure correlates well with the clinical severity of the disease. However, the genotype-phenotype correlation is not absolute and there is clinical variability even within families.

These disorders can also be classified into five groups based on the compromised metabolic pathway: those related to collagen synthesis, structure, and processing; post-translational modification; folding and cross-linking; mineralization; and osteoblast differentiation.

Sclerostin, a glycoprotein primarily derived from osteocytes, was examined in adults with OI enrolled in an RCT. Sclerostin levels were lower in those with type I, III or VI OI compared to age- and sex-matched controls and the level increased in patients with type I OI during teriparatide therapy compared to placebo.
Prenatal ultrasound may detect limb abnormalities in severe cases. C
Prenatal genetic studies should be considered in pregnancies at risk for OI.C
Perform postpartum radiographs in infants at risk of OI to look for beaded ribs, long-bone deformities, and numerous fractures. C
The diagnosis of OI may be suspected at different life stages, including prenatally (in severe cases), at birth, during childhood, or even appearing as late as early adulthood. C

Regardless of the time the diagnosis is suspected, the first line of evaluation includes a detailed medical and family history, physical examination to identify classic OI findings (blue sclera, dentinogenesis imperfecta, short stature, joint hyperlaxity, premature osteopenia, hearing impairment, or skin changes), directed radiographs and lab testing. C

It is essential that OI be distinguished from child abuse, as pathological fractures occur frequently in children with OI, and parents of these children often face charges of abuse which can be devastating. B
Collagen synthesis analysis using cultured dermal fibroblasts and genetic testing for COL1A1, COL1A2, CRATP, LEPRE1 and PRIB mutations are used to make a definitive diagnosis and classify OI. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Extremely short limbs, narrow chest, disproportionately small ribcage, bowing of long bones, enlarged head, prominent wide-spaced eyes
Distinguished by short limbs, small body, absent ossification of spine and pelvis, and narrowed interpediculate distance
Bowing of the long bones, short legs, dislocated hips, 11 pair of ribs, clubfeet, micrognathia, ambiguous genitalia
Appears normal until the onset of poor feeding and growth, hypomineralization of the skull -manifestations of rickets
Short, bowed limbs, malformed vertebral bodies, scoliosis, phalangeal hypoplasia, club feet
Normal bone mineralization, absence of other OI signs, presence of bruising

list.listitem: A family history of OI may or may not be present, and clinically unaffected parents may have more than one child with dominant OI.
Approximately 65% of individuals with OI were in families in which a prior generation was affected; 35% of cases represent new mutations.
Individuals with recessive OI seldom have a family history.
Individuals who are affected with dominant OI have a 50% risk of transmission with each pregnancy.

Many types of OI have been described. Five groupings by type of collegen defect have been proposed by recent authors, and a listing is available in that reference. summarizes the distinguishing clinical characteristics based on the traditional classification system. A newer reference lists additional types of OI (I-XIX) based on affected gene, inheritance and clinical features.
The evaluation requires familiarity with the natural history and clinical presentation of OI, particularly in infants and toddlers.
In childhood, in the absence of a family history, most children newly diagnosed with OI are identified after one or more fractures, or due to growth deficiency.
Children with OI are usually shorter in stature, and appear younger than their chronological age; intelligence is appropriate for age.
In a retrospective case series of 316 patients with OI, scoliosis was diagnosed in half and mean progression was highest in the group with type III at 6° per year.

Prenatal ultrasound is acknowledged as a reliable modality for the diagnosis of severe forms of OI, and should be offered as early as 13-14 weeks gestation for a pregnancy at risk. It is also the primary tool for prenatal screening.

Prenatal analysis can be performed for pregnancies at risk for all types of OI. Biochemical analysis of type I collagen is possible in cultured chorionic villus sampling (CVS)-obtained cells for qualitative alterations, though not for quantitative defects (OI Type I). Cultured CVS can be used for mutation analysis for all types of OI.
Routine laboratory studies are typically normal, and provide little utility for diagnosis of OI.
Collagen synthesis analysis using cultured dermal fibroblasts and genetic testing for COL1A1, COL1A2, CRATP, LEPRE1, PRIB, and other mutations are used to make a definitive diagnosis and classify OI.

Radiographic findings include generalized osteopenia, long-bone bowing, undertubulation and metaphyseal flaring, gracile ribs, narrow thoracic apex, and vertebral compressions. A severity classification based on vertebral compression, thoracolumbar kyphosis and deformity type is under development.
Bone mineral density studies are not generally useful in diagnosing OI, but do serve to provide a quantitative assessment of the individual's osteoporosis.

High-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) is a noninvasive imaging modality for assessing volumetric BMD and microarchitecture of cancellous and cortical bone and may be useful as a marker of fracture risk. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found radial and tibial HR-pQCT parameters were significantly altered in fracture subjects with differences ranging from -2.6% (95% CI -3.4 to -1.9) in radial cortical volumetric BMD to -12.6% (95% CI -15.0 to -10.3) in radial trabecular volumetric BMD. In addition, fracture-associated differences reported by both prospective and retrospective studies indicated that HR-pQCT can predict incident fracture.

OI should be suspected in children presenting with blue sclera, dentinogenesis imperfecta, short stature, joint hyper laxity, or premature osteopenia, hearing impairment, or skin changes, as well as in children with a history of multiple fractures.
More than 50% of individuals with autosomal dominant OI have a family history of OI, and they have a 50% risk of transmission with each pregnancy.
The parents of a child with recessive OI have a 25% risk of recurrence.
Detecting recurrence of OI prenatally is easiest if the exact collagen mutation in the affected child is known.
Genetic counseling and collagen studies are essential components of complete care for individuals with OI.
Collagen analysis is also useful when the diagnosis is equivocal.
The physical examination varies depending on the severity of the disease (see ).
Audiology examination should begin in children as mixed sensorineural and conductive hearing loss occurs in about 5% of patients in their first and second decade.
Goals of treatment are to prevent fracture, maximize mobility, and manage extra-skeletal complications (e.g., dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, cardiovascular and respiratory compromise).
Management focuses on minimizing deformities, preventing and caring for fractures, and physical therapy. C.
There is no curative treatment. B

Intravenous (IV) and oral bisphosphonates and teriparatide increase BMD but have not been clearly shown to reduce fracture incidence; some data support reduced fractures in children primarily taking IV bisphosphonates. B
Currently, bisphosphonates are the only pharmacological agents used in children for OI; their use remains controversial because of inadequate long-term efficacy and safety data.

The use of bisphosphonates in children is typically reserved for the more severe types of OI, as patients with more extensive disease seem to benefit most from the treatment. There is currently no evidence-based data to recommend treatment with bisphosphonates in mild OI.

The consensus guideline (2018) from the Australian Paediatric Endocrine Group (Bone Mineral Working Group) recommend consideration of IV bisphosphonates for children with severe OI, children with vertebral compression fractures, and children who have had 2 or more long bone fractures annually. 29504223 Once BMD improves, these children should be continued on lower-dose (halved) long-term bisphosphonate to preserve bone strength during growth and then discontinued. Oral bisphosphonates can be considered for those with mild to moderate OI.

Pamidronate has been used and studied most extensively, and there is limited information on the use of oral bisphosphonates and risedronate. In the most recent RCT of 147 children with OI children randomized to risedronate had fewer symptomatic radiographically-confirmed nonvertebral fractures and fewer clinical long-bone fractures at one year than children taking placebo (31% vs 49% and 19% vs 35%, respectively).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs with 557 patients found that bisphosphonates reduced fractures in children (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.66-0.97). There was no significant difference in reducing fractures between oral and IV bisphosphonates. Although the RR for adults was similar with respect to fractures, this difference did not reach significance. Authors of a Cochrane review of 14 trials of both oral and IV bisphophonates found improved lumbar spine BMD but inconclusive evidence of improved clinical status (reduce pain; improve growth and functional mobility) or reduced fractures in people with OI.

However, in a 2-year RCT comparing 70 mg oral alendronate weekly to once-yearly infusion of zoledronic acid in 161 children with OI aged 2 to 16 years, there were similar increases in lumbar spine BMD but more clinical fractures in the alendronate group; clinical fracture rate for IV zolendronic acid had a hazard ratio of 0.23, 95% confidence interval 0.118 to 0.431.
In one case series, 127 femoral fractures occurred in one quarter of 93 children with OI; the pattern of fractures was affected by OI type but not by bisphosphonate exposure.

Bisphosphonates may actually cause over-suppression of bone modeling and remodeling, leading to paradoxical fractures. No bisphosphonate has received an official FDA indication for use in children with OI.
Use of bisphosphonates may also reduce bone pain in children and adolescents with diseases with skeletal involvement, but data are limited primarily to uncontrolled studies of poor quality.

Authors of a systematic review found no significant improvement in function and mobility with oral BP administration based on RCTs, while non-randomized open-label uncontrolled studies demonstrated that oral and intravenous BP administration objectively improved function and mobility.
Osteonecrosis of the jaw has not been reported for children with OI treated with bisphosphonates.

In a study of four children between 1 and 9 years of age with type IV OI who developed fractures while on bisphosphonates, denosumab given as 1 mg per kg body mass every 3 months resulted in hypercalcemia in all four children during active therapy and lumbar spine BMD decreased rapidly in children in the two children whose injections were decreased to an interval of every 6 months.

In a 1-year follow-up study of 10 children with OI caused by mutations in COL1A1/A2 who participated in a phase II trial of denosumab, there was a small decrease in lumbar spine BMD but no change in vertebral shape or mobility.

Recombinant human parathyroid hormone (teriparatide) was shown to improve BMD in an RCT with 79 adults with OI. Those with type I OI exhibited robust BMD increases but there was no observed benefit for those with type III/IV OI. There was no difference in self-reported fractures between the two groups at 18 months. Teriparatide only be effective in adults with mild disease.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies of direct and mixed treatment comparisons concluded that although oral bisphosphonates and teriparatide significantly increase BMD, they were not associated with fracture risk reduction in patients with OI.

Limited data show possible benefit of growth hormone on growth among children with certain subtypes of OI. Growth hormone was evaluated in a sample of 26 children with type III or IV OI. Fourteen of the treated children sustained a 50% or more increase in linear growth over their baseline growth rate, with most responders (10 of 14) having moderate type IV OI.
The goal of surgical intervention in OI is to correct deformity to improve weight bearing, enhance mobility, and decrease the fracture/refracture rate in patients.

Treatment of OI is not curative, but focuses on improving the quality and length of life. The general management of patients with OI focuses on minimizing deformities, caring for fractures, and providing rehabilitative physical therapy.

Surgical intervention involves the placement of intramedullary rods to correct severe bowing of the long bones. Telescoping rods lengthen during growth, and are used in younger children, thereby postponing the need for replacement.
In a small case series of children with OI and olecranon fractures, tension band wiring was more successful than screw fixation.

Post-surgical concerns include delays in fracture healing, prolonged immobilization, and loss of muscle mass and functional strength. Re-operation rates are high, and are related to outgrowing the rods. In a long-term (19 years average) follow-up study of 22 patients following Sheffield telescopic intramedullary rods placement, half required reoperation, ten rods (15%) were exchanged because of rod disengagement due to growth, thirteen rods (20%) were exchanged because of complications, and ten rods (15%) required further surgery other than exchange because of complications; patient satisfaction was high.

Surgical correction of scoliosis via spinal fusion with Harrington rods, improves function and ambulation and maintains alignment for at least 5 years with few complications, and should occur when the curvature is more than 50°.
Although stapes surgery or cochlear implants can improve hearing, many patients with OI will typically still require hearing aids.
Prenatal transplantation of allogeneic mesenchymal stem cells with retransplantation later in life has been accomplished and is under study for fetuses with more severe forms of OI.

In children with OI who have achieved significant upright activity using long-leg braces (hip-knee-ankle-foot orthoses), braces can be withdrawn without a significant decrease in muscle strength, although the number of fractures increases.
All children and adults with OI should be managed by a multidisciplinary team, including physical medicine, and orthopedics.
Families of patients with OI should be referred for genetic counseling.
Patients with mild OI have a normal life expectancy. B
Most individuals, even with severe OI, can attain independent living and self-care skills. B
Seventy-six percent of children with OI who are able to sit independently by 10 months are able to walk as their main means of mobility compared with only 18% of those unable to sit. B
Patients with thoracic, scoliosis exceeding 60° have severe reductions in pulmonary function and quality of life. B

feature.caption: Commonly Observed Clinical Types of Osteogenesis Imperfecta.

tr.td: Mildest and most common form (50% of total OI population)
• Multiple fractures from minimal trauma until growth is completed
• Normal teeth - dentinogenesis imperfecta is rare
• Hearing loss in the early 20s or 30s
Most severe form; lethal in the perinatal period
• Patients have multiple in utero fractures often involving skull, long bones, ribs, and vertebrae
• Patients with very small stature with limb shortening
• Large, hypertrophic callouses in the long bones
